evals.prompt: I'm on the organizing committee for PyForge Day, a community-run, volunteer-organized developer conference in Manchester: one day, two rooms, about 500 attendees, and the schedule is locked a month out and basically never changes. A vendor called EventPulse quoted us $4,800 for a conference app, and their sales deck says 80% of attendees at comparable events install it. The committee is excited - push notifications sound perfect for announcements. We already have the registration email list and nothing else. Can you plan the app rollout for us and decide which announcements should go in-app versus by email?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against the app for this edition, grounded in reach and effort, with the announcement list as the floor channel, the vendor's adoption figure rejected, the app's promotion conditions named and found absent, and message classes established before any roster is fixed.
expectations: Recommends against adopting the event app for this edition instead of planning its rollout.
States the announcement list reaches every registrant by construction while an app reaches only the subset who install it.
Rejects the vendor's 80% install figure, stating no adoption figure exists for community-run events and a vendor's number is not to be accepted.

Names the app's promotion conditions - a signed commitment forcing one, three or more concurrent rooms with a schedule grid changing more than once a day, or an already-owned app with sunk content cost - and finds none applies here.
States the app tops the effort ordering (setup plus standing operations) while losing to the announcement list on reach, so the efficiency ordering never selects it.
Grounds the recommendation in reach and effort rather than in the $4,800 price.
Names the announcement list as the default floor channel for a one-day, two-room, locked-schedule event.
Lists or asks for the message classes the edition will actually send before fixing any channel roster.
If a push-speed channel is judged necessary at all, proposes the chat space over the app, since chat matches the app on speed at lower effort.
Asks whether anything signed (sponsor deliverable, venue system, umbrella platform) forces a channel before closing the decision.
Asks about the effort ceiling - organizer hours before the event and who can watch each channel during it - before adding any channel beyond the list.
Gives every channel retained one stated job and one named owner.
Presents the ranking as a default and re-ranks it against what the event already owns, naming the existing registration email list as the asset that anchors the roster.

evals.prompt: We run DataDays Porto, a two-day analytics conference with about 700 attendees, a livestreamed main track, and a shuttle from the metro to the venue. I used to be an SRE, so I want to do comms properly this year: I'm building a status page with severity levels (operational / degraded / major outage), a subscribe-for-updates form, and we'll publish a public post-mortem after any incident. To keep the page active we'll also post daily logistics there - lunch opening, badge desk hours, that kind of thing. We'll host it on the same server as our registration site since we already pay for it. Can you review the plan and write the severity definitions?
evals.expected_output: A review that keeps the status page for the livestream and shuttle but strips the software-status-page imports: no severity tiers, no subscribe model, no public post-mortem, no logistics on the page, independent hosting, a push always pointing at the page, and timestamped fixed-interval updates with a written resolution.
expectations: Rejects the operational/degraded/major severity taxonomy for the event's status page.
States why the taxonomy fails: an event's disruptions are discrete and human-scale, and classifying adds a step during the minutes with least to spare - message classes replace the tiers.
Rejects the subscribe-for-updates form as assuming a long service relationship nobody has with a two-day conference.
Rejects the public post-mortem and routes the written incident note to the internal debrief instead, because a public cause writeup is a liability when the cause is frequently a person or a supplier.
Keeps the status page itself, because the livestream and the shuttle are things an attendee cannot see the state of for themselves.
States the status page is never a push channel: nobody checks it unprompted, and it only works with a push on another channel pointing at it.
Rejects posting daily logistics (lunch, badge desk hours) on the status page because non-incident content trains people to ignore the page.
Routes day logistics to an hours-scale surface such as the chat broadcast channel or on-site screens instead.
Rejects hosting the page on the registration server: the page must survive the outage it reports and stay editable from a phone in under a minute.
Keeps timestamped updates on a fixed interval, including explicit no-change updates, because silence during an outage reads as abandonment.
Keeps a written resolution stating when the incident ended and what actually happened.
Establishes the page as the single canonical surface that every other channel points at rather than restates.
Fixes the update interval before the event and writes it into the routing rule, because an interval chosen during an outage is chosen badly.
Does not write the severity definitions the user asked for.

evals.prompt: TechFest Krakow here - 800 attendees, two days, four tracks, four volunteer writers on comms. Our channel plan for the attendee Discord: #workshop-folks, #talks-only, #speakers, #sponsors, #students and #remote, so every group gets exactly the messages that concern them. For anything urgent, whoever is on duty just DMs the affected people directly. And since about half our audience lives on Telegram, we'll mirror all announcements into a Telegram group too. Sanity-check this before we build it?
evals.expected_output: A rework that replaces the per-segment architecture with a two-channel split, deletes the DM tier and the Telegram mirror outright, moves speaker comms out of the attendee roster, batches sponsor messaging as its own class, and anchors the routing rule on writer operability.
expectations: Rejects the per-audience-segment channel architecture as proposed.
States the operability reason: segment membership is a fresh judgement call on every message, and writers resolve it by cross-posting, which rebuilds the noise the segments were meant to remove.
Recommends the two-channel split - one broadcast channel the event posts on, one open channel where attendees talk - as the default for this shape.
States per-segment channels are legitimate only when segments are genuinely disjoint and stable for the whole event.
Names writer operability as the deciding axis: a volunteer must route a message correctly on the first try with nobody to ask.
Removes direct messages as a routing tier, because a DM leaves no record for the next shift, cannot be escalated, and makes the sender the channel.
Rejects the mirrored Telegram group outright rather than keeping it as a secondary channel: a second chat platform running the same job doubles moderation and halves each announcement's audience.
Routes speaker-facing communication out of the attendee roster to the event's speaker-management function rather than keeping a #speakers channel here.
Handles sponsor messaging as its own message class - batched on email or a dedicated sponsor channel - and never one message per sponsor on the broadcast channel.
Suggests checking whether the chat platform offers a post-only or broadcast mode, which implements the two-channel split at no extra channel cost.
Places the routing rule where the writers are, not in a document opened once.
Gives each surviving channel one stated job and one named owner.
Does not promote the full routing matrix with escalation tiers, since nothing in the brief says the edition is recorded or livestreamed.
Removes the rejected options from the plan entirely rather than demoting them to a lower priority or a backup role.

evals.prompt: Crisis mode at CloudCamp Austin: our venue flooded and we signed a replacement across town yesterday, ten days before the event. I posted the new address in our Discord #announcements channel last night. Is there anything else worth doing? Also, for during the event itself: our main track is livestreamed, and our policy if the stream goes down is to stay quiet until it's fixed so we don't spam people with partial updates. 600 registered, maybe a third are active on the Discord.
evals.expected_output: An escalation of the venue change to every registrant by email plus a canonical update surface and a public-broadcast handoff, a fact-first travel-warning message shape, and a reversal of the silent-outage policy into timestamped fixed-interval updates committed to in advance.
expectations: States that posting the new venue only in Discord is insufficient because the people who need it are not watching chat, with only about a third of registrants active there.
Routes the venue change to the channel that reaches every registrant: email to the full registration list.
Treats the venue change as a class that also goes out publicly, while leaving platform choice and post copy to the public-broadcast or social function.
Recommends one canonical page or surface for venue updates that every other channel points at rather than restates.
Drafts or specifies a venue-change message that opens with an instruction to read it before travelling and states the new address explicitly against the old one.
Puts the new fact before any apology in the message.
Includes a next-update time or a pointer to where further updates will land, since the situation may still change.
Rejects the stay-quiet-until-fixed policy for livestream outages.
States that silence during an outage reads as abandonment, while a still-working-on-it post with a stated next-update time does not.
Requires repeated, timestamped updates at a fixed interval during the outage even when nothing has changed.
Fixes that interval now, before the event, rather than leaving it to be chosen during an outage.
Specifies the livestream outage message commits to posting again by a stated time whether or not the stream is fixed, and notes recordings will still be published.

States the scale rule in both directions: a minutes-scale message never rides an hours-scale channel, and an hours-scale message never rides the disruption path, because the second desensitizes the channel that must not be missed.

Recommends counting every message that has to be re-sent on a second channel because the first did not reach, as a routing or staffing signal, with the ceiling fixed before the event rather than after the data arrives.

evals.prompt: APIcon Amsterdam wrapped five weeks ago. It was explicitly a one-off - the team is dissolving and there will be no next edition. The attendee Slack has 900 members and nobody has moderated it since the closing keynote. One board member wants to keep it open as a community space; another wants to just delete the workspace tonight, quietly, so nobody makes a fuss. Since we're based in the Netherlands, can you also tell me how long GDPR allows us to keep the member list?
evals.expected_output: An export-plus-scheduled-deletion wind-down with the date announced on the channel first, both board proposals rejected on stated grounds, a refusal to quote any retention period with the question routed to counsel alongside a review list, and the unstaffed code-of-conduct duty flagged.
expectations: Recommends export plus scheduled deletion as the wind-down rung, because the edition is a one-off.
States a one-off's member list is a liability with no next edition to spend it on.
Rejects deleting the workspace quietly tonight: a silent wind-down destroys the belief that announcements posted on the event's channels are real.
Requires the deletion date to be announced on the channel itself ahead of time, saying what will be exported and what will not.
Rejects keeping the space open as a community while nobody is on duty: an unmoderated space in the event's name is a code-of-conduct obligation with no responder.
States a hand-off to a community space requires both a compounding series and a named person committed to running the receiving space, and neither holds here.
Declines to state a GDPR retention period or any jurisdiction-specific rule, and routes the retention decision to the organizer's own counsel.

Hands counsel a review list covering the lawful basis for keeping the member list, how long it may be kept, whether moving people requires new consent, the platform's export terms, who holds the ongoing moderation duty, and whether attendees included minors.
Limits the export to what there is a basis to keep: the member list only with such a basis, plus decisions taken, unanswered questions, and post-event content links.
Stores the export under the same basis as the original data and records who can reach it.
Deletes on the announced date including invites, integrations, and any mirror.
Verifies the deletion actually happened, since a scheduled deletion nobody checked is leave-open with paperwork.
Posts a final message with a forwarding address - where to go next and who to contact - and sends the wind-down notice on every channel being closed plus email.
Flags that the code-of-conduct duty on the space has been live and unstaffed for the five weeks since the event ended.

evals.prompt: Five of us write attendee updates for DevSummit Oslo, and two are brand-new volunteers this year. Attendees joke that our channels sound like five different conferences. Our head of comms wants to fix it by personally approving every message before it goes out, including during the event days. Meanwhile our Discord person has settled into a jokey style and our email person writes like a lawyer - honestly, each channel having its own personality feels kind of natural? Also, every edition we send the same three messages: a 'venue closes at 22:00' warning, a 'lunch is ready' ping, and a 'next session starts in 5 minutes' call. We have a written voice guide from our brand work last year. How should we organize all this?
evals.expected_output: A consistency process built on a shared quick-reference plus a pre-written message bank, with blanket live sign-off rejected, per-channel personalities removed, the existing voice guide treated as the fixed register, and the three recurring messages scripted against literal timestamps in advance.
expectations: Rejects blanket pre-publish approval during event days, because sign-off tops consistency but bottoms speed, which hurts most at a live event.

Names the conditions that would justify editorial sign-off - a recorded, livestreamed or press-covered edition, a sponsor contract fixing verbatim wording, or most writers never having seen the register - rather than dismissing it flat.
States that even where sign-off applies, time-critical message classes are exempted to pre-written templates.
Recommends a shared quick-reference condensing the existing voice guide into do/don't lines and worked examples as the base layer.
Escalates to a pre-written message bank because two writers have never written for this event before.
Specifies the bank covers the predictable classes: delay, room change, last call, closing, and similar.
States why the bank works: a frozen template beats a human who drifts, on the messages that actually go out during the event.
For the three recurring clock-based messages, prescribes writing the whole day's script against literal timestamps in advance rather than keeping templates on standby.
Removes the per-channel personalities: a channel-local register invented by whoever writes that channel is deleted, because the event's identity is fixed and only its expression modulates.
Treats the existing voice guide as the fixed register to execute and does not originate a new one.
If a named owner per channel is proposed, states its cost: a slower message whenever the owner is away.
Recommends a humanizing or readability pass on attendee-facing template copy.
Keeps the templates as field sets to be voiced in the register, not finished copy.

evals.prompt: It's 2:30am during NightHack Berlin, our overnight hackathon. A harassment incident happened around 2am and screenshots are already circulating on X. Our social media volunteer has drafted a holding statement and wants to post it on our Discord and on X right now to get ahead of the story - our comms rota says whoever is on shift posts. Our code of conduct team is awake and handling the report. Should the volunteer post? And for next time, should we add an anonymous #incident-reports channel to our Discord so people can flag things without DMing an organizer?
evals.expected_output: A clear no: one authorized publisher named by the code-of-conduct authority, no speed exception, every other channel silent, the on-shift rule corrected for this class only, the anonymous reporting channel kept out of the comms roster, and confirmation that the reporting path covers the Discord.
expectations: Tells the volunteer not to post the holding statement.
States a public statement after an incident has exactly one authorized publisher, and nobody else posts about it on any channel.
Allows no exception for speed: being faster does not authorize a second publisher.
Places the authority over who publishes and what is said with the code-of-conduct function, not with the comms rota.
Corrects the whoever-is-on-shift-posts rule for the incident-statement class specifically, while leaving it intact for routine classes.
States the statement's deadline is set by that authority, not by the comms team or the social media cycle.
Keeps every other channel silent on the incident rather than restating, teasing, or acknowledging the statement in parallel.

Rejects adding an anonymous #incident-reports channel to the comms roster, because incident reporting paths, including anonymous ones, belong to the code-of-conduct function and are excluded from this roster.
Requires confirming that the existing reporting path covers the Discord, without designing the path itself.
Recommends the routing rule or matrix carry an incident-statement row naming the authorized publisher, so the rule survives shift changes.
Does not draft the public statement's copy.
Notes the code of conduct applies inside the Discord and must be stated at the join point, with someone on duty to act on reports - including overnight at an overnight event.
Does not pick which public platform the eventual statement goes out on.

evals.prompt: Last year we ran a student hackathon and the Discord worked great, so for ShipIt Conf - our new one-day, single-track, 300-person developer conference - we cloned the same server template: #team-formation, #carpool-search, #ask-mentors, #mentors-internal, #introductions, #random, #ask-organizers and #admin. We're also building a 'channels' page on a fresh microsite that lists what each channel is for. Our marketing lead already maintains a comms hub page on the main event site from the ticket-sales push. Two of us will run comms. Anything you'd change?
evals.expected_output: A roster rebuilt from the conference's own message classes: hackathon-only channels cut, organizer coordination moved off the attendee server, the chat space itself challenged against its promotion conditions, the second directory page dropped in favor of the existing comms hub, and a dated wind-down chosen before the event.
expectations: Removes #team-formation and #carpool-search: they exist because hackathon attendees must organize each other before the event, and a conference attendee arrives with nothing to form.

Removes or reassigns #ask-mentors and #mentors-internal: they presuppose a mentor population, and the conference's equivalent population is speakers, whose communication belongs to the speaker-management function.
Keeps the transferable discipline: one stated job per channel and a minimum roster stated up front rather than grown organically.
Keeps the attendee-facing ask-organizers channel separate from organizer coordination, and moves #admin off the attendee-facing roster to the operations side.
States staff coordination never routes onto an attendee channel.
Warns that a roster sized for a multi-day overnight event goes silent at a one-day conference, and a quiet channel later carries the one message that mattered.
Lists the message classes the conference will actually send before finalizing the roster.

Challenges whether the chat space itself is warranted at a one-day single-track event, against its promotion conditions: overnight, multi-day, remote participation, or attendees needing to reach each other.
States the chat space's real cost: moderation is a standing job for the whole lifecycle with a code-of-conduct duty identical to the one in the room, not an hour of setup.
Requires the code of conduct to be stated at the join point of the chat space, not only on the event website.
Rejects the new microsite channels page and extends the marketing lead's existing comms hub page instead of publishing a second, competing directory.
Specifies the directory's content per channel: its name, one-line job, who answers on it, the hours it is watched, and what it is not for with a pointer to the channel that is.
Notes the what-it-is-not-for line is the one most directories omit and the one that routes awkward messages correctly.
Chooses the wind-down for every channel now, before the event, and publishes its date on the channels themselves.
